what_it_does: Computing-in-memory (doing math directly inside the memory chip rather than shuttling data to a separate processor) is a promising way to speed up AI workloads, but designing such chips is hard because the behavior depends on the physics of the memory cells themselves. IMCsim is a software simulation framework that lets researchers model a full system — from the instructions the processor issues, down to what happens inside individual memory cells — without having to build real silicon first. It supports three kinds of memory technology (a type of resistive memory called MRAM, traditional fast on-chip SRAM caches, and purely digital in-memory designs) and has been validated against real test chips made in 22 nm and 28 nm manufacturing processes. It also extends the set of processor instructions (the ISA — the vocabulary a chip understands) to include tensor operations, meaning the chip can natively handle the large multi-dimensional array math that AI models require. This lets designers explore trade-offs between speed, power, and area before committing to expensive fabrication.
